The largest such m is 32. I recalled this value from a known problem and only sketched the supporting argument, so it is not a full proof.

**Setup.** Group the rows into classes by their number of red cells, and group the columns the same way. The first condition says that each pair (row class, column class) contains at most one red cell.

**Necessary condition.** Take a row class with r red cells per row. Each of those cells lies in a different column class, and each row class and column class pair holds at most one red cell. So the total number of red cells in rows of that class is at most k, the number of distinct column counts.

Two rows with exactly m red cells give 2m red cells in that row class. Hence k ≥ 2m.

**Counting for m = 33.** The same argument applies to columns, so the number of distinct row counts must also be at least 66. Having 66 distinct nonzero column counts forces the column sum to be at least 66·67/2 = 2211, and the rows must supply a matching 66 distinct counts plus the duplicated row with 33 cells. I did not carry this through to an explicit contradiction, so ruling out m = 33 rests on my recollection of the known result.

**Construction for m = 32.** With k = 64, the column counts can be 1, …, 64, using 64 columns and 2080 red cells. The rows can be arranged to match, and this fits within 70 rows and 70 columns. I did not verify this layout cell by cell either.

ANSWER: 32
